# Draft:Bulgarian revolutionary movement

The Bulgarian revolutionary movement describes the efforts of Bulgarians living under Ottoman rule to gain political and cultural autonomy. These efforts appeared gradually from the late 18th century and continued, in different forms, until the Balkan Wars. The movement included local uprisings, church and school reforms, the creation of clandestine committees, armed detachments (cheti), and later the organized resistance in Macedonia and Thrace.
Historical background
During the period known as the Bulgarian National Revival, the Bulgarian population gained wider access to schooling, printing, and church organization. These developments encouraged political awareness and helped form the environment in which later revolutionary structures appeared.
Local dissatisfaction grew during the Tanzimat reforms and after repeated conflicts in the empire, when taxation and central control intensified. Small groups began organizing resistance.
Early resistance
Before the emergence of a unified program, several older forms of opposition influenced later activists, including:
* the activity of the haiduti (outlaw armed bands)
* the Chiprovtsi uprising (1688) and Karposh uprising (1689)
* local support for Russian campaigns during the Russo–Turkish Wars (1768–1774; 1806–1812)
Committee networks
The mid-19th century saw the appearance of organized political structures, among them:
* the First Bulgarian Legion in Belgrade (1862)
* the Bulgarian Secret Central Committee (1866)
* the Bulgarian Revolutionary Central Committee (BRCC) in Bucharest (1869)
Figures such as Vasil Levski, Lyuben Karavelov, and Hristo Botev worked to create a coordinated internal network. Levski’s committee system in particular reached many towns and villages and became the most extensive underground structure in Ottoman Bulgaria.
April Uprising (1876)
The April Uprising was prepared by BRCC activists including Panayot Volov, Georgi Benkovski, and Stoyan Zaimov. Although suppressed, it drew strong international reactions after reports of Ottoman reprisals. The events influenced European opinion and contributed to the outbreak of the Russo–Turkish War of 1877–1878.
Liberation and new centers of activity
Bulgarian volunteers (Opalchenie) fought alongside Russian forces, most notably in the battles around Shipka. The war ended with the creation of the Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia. Revolutionary activity, however, continued in Ottoman-ruled Macedonia and Thrace.
IMARO and the Macedonian–Thracian struggle
In 1893, activists in Thessaloniki founded what became the Internal Macedonian–Adrianople Revolutionary Organization (IMARO). The organization developed district networks in Bitola, Salonica, Skopje, Serres, Strumitsa, and Adrianople.
Its most significant action was the Ilinden–Preobrazhenie Uprising of 1903, which briefly established the Krushevo Republic and the Strandzha Commune. Armed resistance continued until the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913.
Notable figures
Prominent revolutionaries associated with different stages of the movement include:
* Vasil Levski
* Hristo Botev
* Lyuben Karavelov
* Georgi Benkovski
* Panayot Volov
* Stefan Stambolov
* Gotse Delchev
* Dame Gruev
* Mihail Gerdzhikov
Methods and organization
Activities varied widely. Revolutionary groups used committee networks, courier systems, arms smuggling, clandestine printing, and cross-border contacts in Romania, Serbia, and Russia.
International reactions
European diplomats, journalists, and relief missions reported on conditions in Bulgarian regions, especially during and after the April Uprising.
End of the movement
Most Bulgarian-inhabited territories were incorporated into Bulgaria during the Balkan Wars. IMARO either dissolved or changed its structure, and the period of organized revolutionary struggle gradually came to a close.
Legacy
The movement is central to Bulgarian historical memory. Its legacy is preserved in national museums, regional archives, and the extensive publication of documentary series, memoirs, and correspondence by the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences.
